one_liner: Postgres table-access-method extension (Citus Columnar fork) adding compressed columnar storage, parallel scans, vectorized filters; ~23x vs heap on ClickBench.
what_it_does: A PostgreSQL 13-16 extension named `columnar` that adds a columnar table access method: you write `CREATE TABLE ... USING columnar` (or convert with `columnar.alter_table_set_access_method`) and then query with ordinary SQL, mixing columnar and heap tables or partitions in the same database. It is aimed at analytic scans and aggregates over large, append-mostly tables such as events, logs and clickstream data, and it is not a replacement for heap on OLTP tables. The repo also builds a Docker image meant as a drop-in for the official postgres image. That image sets the database's default_table_access_method to columnar, so every new table is columnar unless you say `USING heap`.
how_it_is_fast: Storage comes from Citus Columnar. Rows are written in stripes of up to 150k rows, and each stripe is split into chunk groups of 10k rows. Each column is stored separately and compressed with zstd by default (lz4 and pglz are also available). Only the projected columns are read, and per-chunk min/max 'skip lists' let WHERE clauses skip whole chunk groups. Hydra adds a parallel-aware CustomScan in which worker processes claim whole stripes through an atomic fetch-and-add counter in dynamic shared memory. It also adds vectorized execution: batches of up to 10,000 column values go through typed comparison functions for column-vs-constant predicates, and there are vectorized COUNT/SUM/AVG aggregates (PG14+). These are plain C loops with no explicit SIMD intrinsics. An optional per-backend cache of decompressed chunks also exists (off by default).
when_to_use: You already run PostgreSQL 13-16 and have append-mostly event, log or clickstream tables of tens to hundreds of millions of rows, queried by dashboards with COUNT/SUM/AVG and simple column-vs-constant filters.
Wide, denormalized tables where queries touch only a few columns, so projection pushdown and chunk-group min/max skipping avoid most of the I/O.

You must keep analytics inside the same Postgres as the OLTP heap tables (same SQL, transactions, joins, pg_dump) rather than run a separate engine. A common layout is a partitioned table with heap partitions for recent, hot data and columnar partitions for older data.
Cutting disk footprint of cold data with zstd-compressed columnar storage: the inherited Citus microbenchmark reports 5.4x smaller than heap on a contrived dataset.
Self-hosted analytics replica or sandbox where you can pin to the last release (v1.1.2) and accept an unmaintained engine.
when_not_to_use: Point lookups and 'find by ID' queries, small latency-sensitive transactions, or frequent large UPDATEs. The project FAQ says these are slower than on heap. UPDATE is implemented as delete plus re-insert, and UPDATE/DELETE lock the table, so they run one at a time.

Trickle ingestion (a few rows per transaction). Each insert transaction writes a new stripe, so you end up with many tiny stripes (issue #239), and planning time grows linearly with stripe count (#188) unless you run columnar.vacuum regularly.
You need PostgreSQL 17+ (configure accepts only 13-16), logical replication, foreign keys, or Citus installed in the same cluster (package file conflicts, #154).
High-concurrency analytics. Queries fan out to parallel workers (columnar.min_parallel_processes defaults to 8), and the FAQ warns that this limits concurrent queries.

Anything needing an active upstream. There have been no code commits since 2024-10. An open wrong-results bug (#282: columnar table returns no or incorrect rows when filtered by values from a joined heap table) and a read error (#247) have no fix, and issue comments say the team moved on to pg_duckdb.

integration.dependencies: PostgreSQL 13-16 server with PGXS dev headers, liblz4 and libzstd (both on by default; --without-lz4/--without-zstd). configure also requires libcurl by default, left over from Citus's anonymous-statistics option; no columnar C source uses it, and --without-libcurl turns the check off. safestringlib is vendored.
integration.min_toolchain: Autoconf plus the C compiler PostgreSQL was built with (pg_config --cc); the builder image is Ubuntu 22.04 with gcc. PostgreSQL 13, 14, 15 or 16 only. Vectorized aggregates need PG14+.
integration.platforms: Linux. The Docker images are built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The code uses no explicit SIMD intrinsics; macOS and Windows builds are not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Uses the Postgres process model with no threads. Intra-query parallelism uses parallel worker processes that coordinate through a shared-memory atomic stripe counter. The column cache is per-backend memory. UPDATE/DELETE take a table lock, so concurrent writers serialize. Hydra's docs recommend REPEATABLE READ for stronger isolation; the inherited Citus README lists SERIALIZABLE as unsupported.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same SQL and access-method API: switch a table with USING columnar or alter_table_set_access_method, and the Docker image replaces the postgres image. But only columnar tables get faster. Logical replication, foreign keys and some index or constraint types are unsupported, and write-heavy or point-lookup workloads get slower.

gotchas: The Docker image makes columnar the database-wide default table access method, so lookup and reference tables silently become columnar and slow unless created USING heap. With that default, a large INSERT ... SELECT or CREATE TABLE can still fail with a parallel-operation error (#267, open).

Stripes are fixed at write time. The chunk_group_row_limit and stripe_row_limit options apply only to newly written data. Small transactions fragment the table, and columnar.vacuum reportedly fails to release space from fully deleted stripes (#285). One corrupted stripe raises an error that aborts reads, VACUUM and index builds for the whole table (#284).

Vectorization only fires for column-vs-constant comparisons on basic types (int2/4/8, char, date, time, timestamp[tz]). An OR with any non-vectorizable branch disables it for that branch, and FILTER aggregates are not vectorized. -O3 is opt-in (make COLUMNAR_O3=1) in the current Makefile, and the in-tree src/backend/columnar/README.md is the stale Citus text ('append-only', 'no parallel scans').

The extension is named `columnar`, the same name as Citus Columnar. The two cannot be installed side by side, and there is no supported physical migration from Citus Columnar (#154). The planner may also skip useful indexes on columnar tables; the maintainers suggest pg_hint_plan (#155).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over DataFusion, Databend or chDB when the data must stay inside a running Postgres (same transactions, joins with heap tables, existing tooling) and you only need a few-to-25x speedup on scan-and-aggregate queries. If you can move analytics to a separate engine, those siblings are actively maintained, purpose-built columnar engines. Their catalogued ClickBench totals are single-digit to tens of seconds, though on larger hardware, whereas Hydra totals about 479 s on c6a.4xlarge.
verified_claims_summary: The benchmark is ClickBench on the 100M-row hits table on AWS c6a.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32 GB, 500 GB gp2), with no compiler or flags stated. The README chart puts Hydra about 23x ahead of stock PostgreSQL heap overall, and three labelled queries go from 282.02 s to 0.55 s (COUNT), 263.07 s to 0.93 s (SUM/AVG) and 254.24 s to 0.18 s (filtered COUNT). ClickBench's raw files give roughly 25x geometric mean for Hydra 2023-09-19 over the 2022-07-01 PostgreSQL run (faster on all 43 queries). Against the newer 2025-02-26 PostgreSQL run the result is roughly parity on ClickBench's +10 ms geometric mean: Hydra is slower on 19 of 43 queries, though its summed hot time of about 479 s is still about 7.7x lower than PostgreSQL's 3,675 s (derived).
status_note: Stale and effectively abandoned. The last code change was 2024-10-07, the last commit (README) 2025-02-10 and the last release v1.1.2 (2024-04-01), with no PG17 support and open correctness bugs. The engine under columnar/ is AGPL-3.0, whose network-use copyleft matters for hosted products, and the rest of the repo is Apache-2.0. It is buildable from source or usable via the published Docker images.
